t: Ba'athism joined Arab nationalism to a socialism that rejected Marxist class struggle, and held that a vanguard Ba'ath party should rule for an unspecified time to build an "enlightened" Arab society.
The founders' party split in 1966 into a Syrian-dominated and an Iraqi-dominated movement, and the Assad family and Saddam Hussein built personalist dictatorships in the two countries.
Both Ba'athist regimes built police states with mass surveillance and ideological indoctrination, and both fell: Iraq's in the invasion of 2003, Syria's on 8 December 2024.
dyk: Michel Aflaq, a Christian, called the rise of Islam in the seventh century the first Arab renaissance; when he died in 1989 the Iraqi Regional Command announced that he had converted to Islam, but his family was said not to know of any conversion.
ev: Zaki al-Arsuzi founds the Arab Ba'ath on 29 November, and Michel Aflaq and Salah al-Din al-Bitar found the Arab Ihya Movement, later the Arab Ba'ath Movement
The first party congress meets, the two Ba'ath movements merge, and the party adopts its charter
The Military Committee of the Syrian Ba'ath party launches a coup that sets up a one-party state in Syria
A second Syrian coup overthrows the old guard led by Aflaq and Bitar and splits the movement into a Syrian and an Iraqi wing
The Iraqi Ba'ath seizes power in a coup and later gives asylum to Aflaq
The Corrective Revolution puts Hafez al-Assad in power in Syria
The invasion of Iraq topples Saddam Hussein, and the Iraqi Ba'ath party is banned
The Assad regime falls on 8 December, ending Ba'athist rule in Syria

f.thinkers: Michel Aflaq, generally counted its founder or chief contributor; Salah al-Din al-Bitar, who worked directly with Aflaq; Zaki al-Arsuzi, who influenced Aflaq and founded the Arab Ba'ath; Hafez al-Assad, whose policies gave rise to Assadism; Saddam Hussein, whose politics gave rise to Saddamism
f.texts: Aflaq's essay compilation Fi Sabil al-Ba'ath (The Road to Renaissance, 1940), the party's main ideological book for more than two decades; the Ba'ath Party Charter of 1947, whose Articles 26–37 set out its socialism
f.ideas: Arab nationalism and the unity of the Arab nation; baʽth, the renaissance of Arab culture, values and society; a vanguard party ruling for an unspecified time; Arab socialism with state ownership of natural resources and the principal means of production; revolution against the reactionary classes; a secular state with Islam kept spiritual; the slogan "Unity, Freedom, Socialism"
f.today: Both Ba'athist regimes fell: Iraq's in 2003 and Syria's on 8 December 2024; the Ba'ath party in Syria was dissolved in 2025, few Ba'athist groups remain elsewhere with limited influence, and organisations linked to the party in Lebanon face forced dissolution by the government
